patterns.usage_note: A sentence-final reproach: だろうが or でしょうが presses on the hearer a fact the speaker treats as obvious, complaining that they should have known it (だから言っただろうが, 危ないでしょうが). The other entry for this form is the concessive, which brushes a condition aside mid-sentence (誰が反対しようが, 学生だろうが). Sentence-final position is what fixes this reading; the tone is blunt and confrontational.

examples.ruby: 傘[かさ]を持[も]って行[い]けとあれほど言[い]っただろうが。
examples.english: I told you over and over to take an umbrella!

examples.ruby: 今[いま]のは誰[だれ]が見[み]てもファウルだろうが。
examples.english: Anyone could see that was a foul!

examples.ruby: その鍵[かぎ]は昨日[きのう]あなたに渡[わた]したでしょうが。
examples.english: But I gave you that key yesterday!

patterns.usage_note: Presses a judgment the speaker treats as obvious onto the hearer as a question, most often as reproach or complaint (確認すると言ったじゃないか, まだ子供じゃないか). The sibling lane is the falling-tone exclamation of surprise or admiration at something just noticed (鍵はここにあるじゃないか). Polite じゃないですか often only invites the hearer to confirm shared knowledge, with no blame; after a volitional it is an invitation (行こうじゃないか).

examples.ruby: 昨日[きのう]ちゃんと確認[かくにん]すると言[い]ったじゃないか。
examples.english: You told me yesterday you'd double-check it, didn't you!

examples.ruby: そんなに怒[おこ]らなくても、あの子[こ]はまだ子供[こども]じゃないか。
examples.english: Go easy on her; she's still just a kid, come on.

examples.ruby: そんな大声[おおごえ]で話[はな]したら、周[まわ]りの人[ひと]に迷惑[めいわく]じゃないか。
examples.english: Talk that loudly and you're bothering everyone around us, come on.
